title: parseInt("1e3") is 1, but Number("1e3") is 1000
assumption: parseInt and Number agree on what a numeric string means; parseInt is just 'the integer version'.

input.description: Converting a user-entered or CSV-sourced numeric string that happens to be in scientific notation (common in spreadsheet exports of large or small numbers).

what_goes_wrong: Switching a 'parse this numeric string' call from `Number()` to `parseInt()` (e.g. 'because I want an integer') silently truncates any value written in scientific notation to just its leading digit, turning 1000 into 1 with no error.
why: `parseInt` parses a string by reading characters strictly left to right and stopping at the first character that cannot extend a valid integer literal in the given radix -- it has no concept of an exponent, so it stops at the "e". `Number()` instead parses the whole string against ECMA-262's StringNumericLiteral grammar (similar to, but not the same as, source-code numeric literals: it allows surrounding whitespace and "Infinity", and rejects numeric separators and the `n` BigInt suffix), which does understand exponents, so it parses "1e3" as 1 * 10^3 = 1000. The two are not interchangeable string-to-number converters.

repros.expected_output:
int('1e3') ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '1e3'
1000.0

fix: Use `Number()` (and then validate/round) to parse a numeric string that might contain an exponent, decimals, or thousands separators; reserve `parseInt` for strings you know are plain digit sequences in a known radix.

sources.title: ECMA-262: ToNumber applied to the String type

test_cases.note: Decide explicitly whether a numeric-string parser should understand scientific notation; don't silently truncate at the exponent.
